title: Delhi Court Acquits Former WFI Chief Brij Bhushan Singh in Wrestlers' Sexual Harassment Case
excerpt: The verdict ends a three-year legal battle sparked by allegations from six female wrestlers, though the complainants have vowed to appeal.
body:
• A Delhi court acquitted former Wrestling Federation of India chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh and co-accused Vinod Tomar of all sexual harassment charges on August 3, 2026.
  • Six women wrestlers had accused Singh of harassment between 2016 and 2019; charges were framed in May 2024 under multiple IPC sections.
  • Olympic wrestler Vinesh Phogat said the complainants will appeal, stating they "have not lost hope."

A Delhi court on Monday acquitted former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief and BJP leader Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh of all sexual harassment charges brought by female wrestlers, ending a criminal case that had fueled months of nationwide protest in 2023 and forced a reckoning with abuse in Indian sport.

Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Ashwini Panwar of the Rouse Avenue Courts pronounced the verdict, acquitting both Singh and co-accused Vinod Tomar, the former WFI assistant secretary who faced charges of criminal intimidation and abetment, according to Reuters.

"I had complete faith that justice would be done… justice was done. I never considered myself a criminal at all."

— Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh, after the verdict

Visuals from news agency ANI showed supporters garlanding Singh, feeding him traditional Indian sweets, and presenting bouquets outside the court.

Background and Charges

The case stemmed from complaints by six women wrestlers alleging that Singh sexually harassed them between 2016 and 2019 at the WFI office in New Delhi, at his official residence, and during overseas tournaments and official engagements. Delhi Police registered an FIR and filed a chargesheet on June 15, 2023, under Sections 354 (outraging modesty), 354A (sexual harassment), 354D (stalking), and 506(1) (criminal intimidation) of the Indian Penal Code.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2084149698076737640

On May 10, 2024, the trial court framed charges against Singh for offences under Sections 354 and 354A in relation to five complainants and under Section 506(1) concerning two wrestlers. He was discharged regarding the sixth complainant. Tomar faced charges only under Section 506(1) for criminal intimidation related to one complainant.

A separate POCSO case filed by a minor wrestler was earlier closed after the complainant withdrew her allegations and Delhi Police filed a cancellation report.

The 2023 Protests That Shook Indian Sport

The allegations triggered one of the most high-profile protests in Indian sports history. Olympic wrestling star Vinesh Phogat, Olympic medallists Sakshi Malik and Bajrang Punia, and hundreds of other athletes staged a sit-in demonstration in New Delhi in 2023 demanding criminal action against Singh. Punia returned one of India's highest civilian awards, while Malik announced her retirement from competitive wrestling in protest.

The demonstrations drew widespread public support and put pressure on the ruling BJP, since Singh was at the time a sitting Member of Parliament from the party. He completed his term in 2024 and was not renominated; the BJP fielded his son for the same constituency, where he won and currently serves as a lawmaker.

Wrestlers Vow to Appeal

The acquittal is unlikely to be the final word. Phogat said on X that the women wrestlers had instructed their lawyer to appeal the verdict and the process would begin "as soon as possible."

"We have not lost hope, and the wrestlers will continue their fight."

— Vinesh Phogat, on X

Senior Advocate Rebecca John, who appeared for the complainant wrestlers throughout the trial, is expected to file the appeal in a higher court. Legal observers note that in-camera trial proceedings — conducted behind closed doors — limit public scrutiny of the evidence and reasoning, making the appellate stage critical for transparency.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the case has been a touchstone in wider conversations about accountability, gender-based violence, and the intersection of politics and sport in India. The 2023 protests resonated globally, with diaspora groups organizing solidarity events. The acquittal — and the promised appeal — will likely renew those discussions, particularly among communities tracking women's safety and institutional reform in India.

What's Next

The complainants' legal team is expected to move the appellate court in the coming weeks. The outcome of the appeal could reshape how sexual harassment cases involving powerful public figures are prosecuted in India. Meanwhile, the WFI remains under scrutiny; the federation was suspended by United World Wrestling in 2023 over governance concerns and has struggled to regain full autonomy.
